screens.title: Introduction to DApps and Web3.js
screens.subtitle: Understand how frontends connect to the Ethereum blockchain using Web3.js

narration.text: Welcome. In this chapter you will learn what makes a Decentralized Application different from a traditional web app and how Web3. js serves as the essential bridge between your frontend and the Ethereum network. A DApp keeps backend logic in on-chain smart contracts rather than a centralized server, which gives you transparency and immutability but also introduces new development patterns. We will look at the typical DApp stack: a browser-based frontend, Web3. js as the client library, an Ethereum node as the gateway, and the blockchain where contracts live. You will also set up a simple project, install Web3. js, and initialize a connection to a local Ganache node to verify you can read blocks and accounts. Along the way we’ll highlight provider types — HTTP, WebSocket, IPC, and injected providers like MetaMask — and why you would choose one for reads, subscriptions, or user-signed transactions. Expect hands-on steps that include creating a Node project, installing Web3. js, and running a short script that fetches the latest block and accounts. By the end you’ll understand the data flow and be ready to perform basic contract calls and transactions. Think about a simple question as you start: what part of your app needs on-chain trust, and what can stay in the frontend?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Web3.js is the JavaScript bridge that lets a frontend speak to Ethereum nodes, enabling DApps to read blockchain state and submit signed transactions.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Introduction to DApps and Web3.js
Introduction to DApps and Web3.js
How frontends communicate with Ethereum and why that matters for DApp design.

A DApp combines a familiar web frontend with smart-contract logic on-chain. Web3.js is the client library that lets JavaScript call contract methods, query blocks, and submit transactions through an Ethereum node. This chapter gives you the setup, sample code, and essential provider choices for early DApp development.

In this lesson
You will set up a Node project, install Web3.js, connect to a Ganache node, and verify results using getBlockNumber and getAccounts. We emphasize provider types and correct async patterns.
Architecture
Frontend → Web3.js → Node → Blockchain
Setup
Node, npm, npm install web3
Verify
getBlockNumber, getAccounts
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Visual: Flow Cards
Cards show each runtime role: browser, library, node, blockchain.
Frontend
HTML/JS app that needs blockchain data.
Web3.js
Client library that speaks to the node.
Node
An Ethereum client exposing RPC endpoints.
Blockchain
Immutable state and smart contracts.
Coming up
We’ll walk through npm install web3, creating connect.js, and running a local Ganache node to verify connection. Expect concrete code and terminal output you can reproduce.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Part 1
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: In this section we list concrete objectives you'll reach by working through the exercises. First, you will be able to explain a DApp's architecture: what lives in the frontend versus what runs on-chain. Being precise about that separation helps you design for immutability and gas costs. Second, you'll understand the role of Web3. js as the client-side library that converts JavaScript calls into RPC calls understood by an Ethereum node. This matters because a DApp's ability to read contract state or submit transactions depends entirely on that bridge. Third, you'll set up a basic development environment using Node. js and npm, and install the Web3. js package. This is practical work: initializing a project directory, running npm commands, and managing dependencies. Fourth, you'll install Web3. js in a way that fits both Node and browser workflows so you can test locally before deploying. Each objective is tied to hands-on steps: design thinking for architecture, A P I literacy for Web3. js, and practical setup work that ensures your machine can run a local Ganache node. Keep these goals in mind as checkpoints you can verify by running small scripts that fetch block numbers and accounts.

keyIdea.title: Objective focus
keyIdea.text: These skills combine conceptual design with practical setup so you can move from idea to a running DApp prototype.

narration.text: This second objectives screen focuses on the practical skills you'll apply and how to verify them. First, you'll initialize a Web3. js instance and connect it to an Ethereum node. This is the step where you provide a provider URL or use an injected wallet so your JavaScript can reach the network. Second, you will be able to differentiate provider types — HTTP for simple requests, WebSocket for subscriptions and real-time updates, IPC for local server processes, and injected providers like MetaMask for user account management. Knowing the trade-offs will help you pick the right approach for reads, writes, and user interactions. Third, you'll practice handling asynchronous operations: Web3. js methods return Promises, so you must use async/await or. then to fetch results reliably. Finally, you will verify your connection using a local Ganache instance by running a small script that prints the network ID, latest block, accounts list, and an account balance converted to Ether. These verification steps are practical tests that confirm your environment and Web3. js configuration are correct.

screens.title: What is a Decentralized Application (DApp)?
screens.subtitle: Definition, properties, and a practical analogy

narration.text: A Decentralized Application, or DApp, is an application where the backend logic runs on a decentralized blockchain rather than a single server. This design gives you three important properties: immutability, because the blockchain stores a tamper-resistant record; transparency, because state transitions are visible to observers; and censorship resistance, because no single party can unilaterally take down on-chain logic. Practically, a DApp still uses a familiar frontend built with H T M L and JavaScript, but instead of calling centralized APIs, it calls smart contracts deployed on the blockchain. Think of the frontend as a storefront and smart contracts as vending machines: the frontend presents the UI, but the vending machine enforces product rules and payments without a store manager. One common misconception is assuming all DApp data must be on-chain — costly and unnecessary. Often you keep large, mutable data off-chain and store essential state or settlement logic on-chain. For example, a token transfer should be on-chain for trust, but user profile pictures can be hosted off-chain with a content hash on-chain. Key takeaway: design what truly needs blockchain guarantees versus what can remain in the frontend to save cost and complexity. How does that mapping change the way you test and deploy a feature in your app?

keyIdea.title: DApp essence
keyIdea.text: Keep critical rules and settlement on-chain; keep heavy or mutable assets off-chain and reference them when needed.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › What is a DApp?
Decentralized Application (DApp)
Backend logic runs on smart contracts; frontend remains a web app.
  • Immutability: On-chain rules are tamper-resistant when deployed.
  • Transparency: State changes are visible on the chain.
  • Censorship resistance: No single operator controls contract execution.
Analogy
Frontend = storefront; smart contract = vending machine enforcing payments and rules.
Misconception
Not everything belongs on-chain. Large assets and mutable data usually stay off-chain.
Key Takeaway

Place only rules and settlement on-chain. Keep heavy or frequently changing data off-chain and reference it with hashes when needed.

Definition & example
Example: A token transfer is enforced by a smart contract transfer method so the ledger is authoritative. User avatars and large media remain on standard hosting, with a content hash stored on-chain for integrity verification.
Check your understanding
Which elements require on-chain trust? Think about money, ownership, and settlement logic.
Which elements can be off-chain to save gas costs? Consider images, large documents, and transient UI state.

screens.title: What is Web3.js?
screens.subtitle: The client-side library that speaks Ethereum

narration.text: Web3. js is a collection of JavaScript libraries that allow your frontend code to interact with an Ethereum node over HTTP, WebSocket, or IPC. It exposes a high-level A P I for common blockchain tasks: querying the current block number, listing accounts, reading contract state, sending transactions, and subscribing to events. Think of Web3. js as a translator: it converts JavaScript method calls into the JSON-RPC requests that nodes understand and turns JSON-RPC responses into JavaScript-friendly data. Practically, you use Web3. js to call web3. eth. getBlockNumber, web3. eth. getAccounts, web3. eth. getBalance, and to create contract instances that let you call methods defined in your smart contract ABI. A frequent beginner pitfall is assuming Web3. js synchronous behavior; most calls return Promises, so you must await them or use. then. Another nuance is environment differences: in Node you require or import Web3, while in the browser you may use a bundler or an injected provider. A concrete example is installing Web3 with npm and creating a simple web3 = new Web3('http://localhost:8545') to read the latest block. That simple step is the foundation for every subsequent contract interaction and transaction flow in your DApp.

keyIdea.title: Web3.js role
keyIdea.text: Web3.js translates JavaScript calls to Ethereum node RPCs, enabling queries, contract calls, transactions, and event subscriptions.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › What is Web3.js?
Web3.js — client library
Provides APIs for accounts, transactions, contracts, and events.
  • Converts JavaScript calls into JSON-RPC requests the node can execute.
  • Returns asynchronous Promises for most operations.
  • Works with multiple provider types depending on your environment.
Practical example
Install with npm and create a new Web3 instance pointing to a node URL to start making calls.
Quick reference
Common methods you will use:
  • web3.eth.getBlockNumber() — fetch the latest block.
  • web3.eth.getAccounts() — list available accounts.
  • web3.eth.getBalance(address) — get an account balance.
Common pitfall
Assuming synchronous return values. Always await Promises or use .then to access values.

screens.title: Install Web3.js and Initialize a Project
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step setup using npm and project initialization

narration.text: Setting up a development project is the predictable first step. Begin by ensuring you have Node. js and npm installed; these tools let you manage packages and run scripts. In the terminal, create a new directory for your DApp and run npm init -y to generate a package. json file with sensible defaults. Next, install Web3. js with npm install web3. This places Web3 in your dependencies and makes it available for require or import statements. If you're building a simple static page, you could also add Web3 via a CDN, but using npm is standard for modern frameworks. Once installed, you can create a file like connect. js with starter code that requires Web3 and instantiates a new Web3 object with a provider URL. This process establishes a local, reproducible environment suitable for testing against Ganache or a hosted provider. It also keeps your project consistent across team members and CI environments. A common misconception is that installation alone is enough — you must also verify the library works by running a short script that calls getBlockNumber or getAccounts. That verification step ensures your node or provider is reachable and your code can parse the responses. Always check package. json after installing to confirm the dependency.

keyIdea.title: Setup pattern
keyIdea.text: Use npm to manage Web3.js so your project is reproducible; verify the installation by running a small script that calls the node.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Install Web3.js and Initialize
Project setup steps
Create a reproducible environment for your DApp with npm.
Terminal steps
npm init -y
npm install web3
These commands create package.json and add Web3 as a dependency. Confirm package.json lists web3 under dependencies.
Why npm?
npm ensures consistent versions across environments and makes it easy to bundle Web3 into your frontend build.
Verification
Run a quick script that requires Web3 and calls getBlockNumber to ensure connectivity.
Common mistake
Skipping verification or using mismatched package versions can cause runtime errors later in development.

screens.title: Initialize Web3.js and Connect to a Node
screens.subtitle: Create a Web3 instance and run basic sanity checks

narration.text: Initializing Web3. js is a small but crucial step. You construct a Web3 object and give it a provider string or object that tells it how to reach a node. In Node. js you might require Web3 and call new Web3('http://localhost:8545') to point at a local Ganache instance. After creating the instance, test connectivity with web3. eth. getBlockNumber and web3. eth. getAccounts. These methods are asynchronous and return Promises, so use async/await or. then to access their values. A short pattern is to wrap calls in an async function and catch errors so you can diagnose network issues. If you see a connection error, ensure your node is running and the URL matches its RPC endpoint. Avoid exposing secret project IDs in client-side code if you use a hosted provider; prefer environment variables and server-side proxies for secrets. The following code is a minimal example you can paste into connect. js to verify your environment. Running this script confirms that your Web3 instance can query the node and retrieve both the block number and available accounts, a foundational verification step for further contract calls.

keyIdea.title: Initialize & verify
keyIdea.text: After creating a Web3 instance, always run simple async checks like getBlockNumber and getAccounts to ensure the provider is reachable.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Initialize Web3.js
Minimal connect.js
Run with node connect.js after installing web3 and running Ganache.
const Web3 = require('web3');
const web3 = new Web3('http://localhost:8545');

async function getBlockNumber() {
  try {
    const blockNumber = await web3.eth.getBlockNumber();
    console.log('Current block number:', blockNumber);

    const accounts = await web3.eth.getAccounts();
    console.log('Available accounts:', accounts);
  } catch (error) {
    console.error('Error connecting to Ethereum:', error.message);
  }
}

getBlockNumber();
This code shows the pattern: create Web3, await calls in an async function, catch errors to diagnose connectivity problems.
Explanation
  • Require or import Web3 depending on environment.
  • Pass a provider URL to the constructor to connect to your node.
  • Wrap calls in async functions and handle promise rejections.
Key Takeaway

A working Web3 instance plus successful getBlockNumber and getAccounts calls confirm a valid provider connection.

screens.title: Provider Types and When to Use Them
screens.subtitle: HTTP, WebSocket, IPC, and Injected (MetaMask)

narration.text: Choosing the right provider is essential because it determines how you communicate with the node and which features you can rely on. The HTTP provider is simple and widely supported: you send JSON-RPC over HTTP. It works well for occasional reads and straightforward transactions, and it's easy to use with local Ganache or hosted endpoints. However, it is not ideal for real-time updates because polling is required. The WebSocket provider creates a persistent connection, enabling subscriptions and push-style updates. Use WebSocket when your DApp needs near real-time events such as new blocks or contract events without continuous polling. IPC is an inter-process communication channel best used when your application and the node run on the same host; it offers performance advantages for local server-side code but is rarely used in browser frontends. Finally, injected providers like MetaMask expose window. ethereum in the browser and handle account management and transaction signing for end users. This is the standard for user-facing DApps because it keeps private keys secure inside the wallet. A common error is attempting to sign transactions with an HTTP provider when you should use an injected provider or a server-side signing strategy. Choose based on needs for subscriptions, signing, and deployment context.

keyIdea.title: Provider selection
keyIdea.text: Use HTTP for simple reads, WebSocket for subscriptions, IPC for local server performance, and injected providers for secure user signing.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Provider Types
Provider comparison
Choose by use case: reads, subscriptions, signing, or local performance.
HTTP Provider
Good for simple RPC calls and local testing. No push updates; polling required for new data.
WebSocket Provider
Persistent connection for subscriptions and real-time events; ideal for dashboards and reactive UIs.
IPC Provider
High-performance local connection used by server-side apps running on the same host as the node.
Injected Provider (MetaMask)
Exposes a browser wallet for account management and secure client-side signing. Standard for user-facing DApps.
When to choose
  • Use HTTP for development reads and simple scripts.
  • Use WebSocket for subscriptions, event-driven UIs, and timely updates.
  • Use IPC for server-side, same-host performance needs.
  • Use injected providers for user-signed transactions and secure private key handling.
Pro tip
When testing with Ganache, use HTTP locally. For a production-facing DApp that needs realtime, add a WebSocket layer or a server push mechanism.

screens.title: Connect to a Local Ganache Node (connect.js)
screens.subtitle: A reproducible script to verify network ID, blocks, accounts, and balances

narration.text: This hands-on script verifies your environment and demonstrates the typical calls you'll use in almost every DApp. After starting Ganache, create a project folder and install Web3. Then save the following code in connect. js and run it with node connect. js. The script constructs a Web3 object pointed at the Ganache RPC URL, queries the network ID to ensure you're on the expected chain, gets the latest block number to confirm sync, lists available accounts, and reads the first account's balance, converting from wei to ether. Each step shows real outputs that you can check in the terminal. If any call fails, the catch block prints a helpful error; common fixes are: Ganache not running, wrong RPC address, or firewall blocking the port. This verification gives you confidence that your frontend can reach a node and that you can reference accounts for transactions. Practice running the script, inspect the printed account address and balance, and reflect on how that account will be used for subsequent contract deployments or transactions. This small reproducible test is the foundation for safe and predictable DApp development.

keyIdea.title: Verify locally
keyIdea.text: Running connect.js against Ganache confirms network connectivity and available accounts, forming the basis for deploying and testing contracts.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Connect to Ganache
connect.js
const Web3 = require('web3');

// --- YOUR GANACHE RPC URL HERE ---
const ganacheRpcUrl = 'http://127.0.0.1:8545';

const web3 = new Web3(ganacheRpcUrl);

async function checkConnection() {
  try {
    const networkId = await web3.eth.net.getId();
    console.log('Successfully connected to network ID:', networkId);

    const latestBlock = await web3.eth.getBlockNumber();
    console.log('Latest block number:', latestBlock);

    const accounts = await web3.eth.getAccounts();
    console.log('First account address:', accounts[0]);

    const balanceWei = await web3.eth.getBalance(accounts[0]);
    const balanceEth = web3.utils.fromWei(balanceWei, 'ether');
    console.log(`Balance of first account: ${'${balanceEth}'} ETH`);

  } catch (error) {
    console.error('Failed to connect to Ganache or fetch data:', error.message);
    console.error('Please ensure Ganache is running and the RPC URL is correct.');
  }
}

checkConnection();
Expected terminal output
Successfully connected to network ID: 5777
Latest block number: 12
First account address: 0x1234...abcd
Balance of first account: 100 ETH
Troubleshooting
  • Confirm Ganache is running and RPC URL matches the displayed address.
  • Check firewall or port conflicts if connection is refused.
  • Ensure web3 package is installed locally in the project.
Key Takeaway

A short verification script gives immediate feedback that your development environment, provider, and Web3.js setup are correct.

screens.title: Asynchronous Operations and Promises in Web3.js
screens.subtitle: Why await and .then matter for reliable DApps

narration.text: Most Web3. js calls are asynchronous because network calls can take unpredictable time. Methods like web3. eth. getBlockNumber or web3. eth. getAccounts return Promises. If you attempt to use their return values synchronously, you will get unresolved Promise objects instead of the expected data. The correct approach is to use async/await inside an async function or chain. then and. catch to handle resolution and errors. For example, await web3. eth. getBlockNumber() will pause execution until the Promise resolves and returns the numeric block value. A common beginner error is omitting await or not returning a Promise from a function, which leads to race conditions where code runs before data is available. Another practical concern is error handling; always wrap awaits in try/catch so network errors do not crash your app unexpectedly. Also consider UX: show loading states while awaiting data and disable transaction buttons until accounts are loaded. These patterns make your DApp predictable and user-friendly. A simple concrete example is fetching the account list and then displaying the first address — if you omit await, the displayed value will be a Promise string rather than the real address. How will you surface loading and error states in your UI?

keyIdea.title: Async discipline
keyIdea.text: Always treat Web3.js calls as asynchronous: use async/await or .then with try/catch and present clear loading/error states to users.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Async Operations & Promises
Pattern: async/await
async function fetchData() {
  try {
    const block = await web3.eth.getBlockNumber();
    console.log('Block:', block);
  } catch (err) {
    console.error('Network error:', err.message);
  }
}
Wrap awaits in try/catch to handle network failures gracefully. Use loading indicators in the UI while promises resolve.
Common mistake
Calling web3.eth.getBlockNumber() without await returns a Promise object, causing code that expects a number to break or display incorrect values.
Key Takeaway

Treat Web3.js calls as asynchronous and design your UI to handle loading, success, and error states clearly.

Check your understanding
How would you prevent a user from sending a transaction before accounts are loaded? Think about disabled buttons and account-ready flags.

screens.title: Common Errors and Security Pitfalls
screens.subtitle: Asynchronous mistakes, provider misconfiguration, and leaking secrets

narration.text: Beginners commonly encounter a small set of repeatable errors that block progress. First, asynchronous mistakes — forgetting to await Promises — lead to undefined or Promise objects in the UI. Second, provider misconfiguration causes connection refusals: a wrong RPC URL or a node that isn't running will make calls fail. Third, security pitfalls include embedding secret provider keys or project IDs in client-side code. Hosted RPC services often provide project secrets; do not expose them in the browser. Use environment variables or a server-side proxy when a secret must be used. Another mistake is attempting to sign transactions using an HTTP provider directly from code without using an injected wallet or server-side signing; private keys must never be committed to client-side code. Also, developers sometimes rely on mainnet endpoints for development — prefer local Ganache or testnets when iterating. The remedy is straightforward: handle Promises explicitly, validate provider URLs, and keep secrets server-side. For signing, prefer injected providers like MetaMask for user-driven actions or server-side signing for controlled backend flows. These habits make your DApp safer and easier to debug.

keyIdea.title: Avoid these errors
keyIdea.text: Handle async correctly, validate providers, and never expose secrets or private keys in client-side code; use injected wallets for user signing.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Common Errors & Security
Async bug
Omitting await causes unresolved Promises. Always await or chain .then to access values.
Provider misconfig
Wrong RPC URL or node offline results in connection refusals. Double-check the endpoint and node status.
Exposing secrets
Never embed private keys or secret project IDs in client-side bundles. Use server proxies or env variables.
Signing transactions
Use MetaMask/injected providers for user signing. Server-side signing is for backend flows under your control.
Test environment
Develop against Ganache or public testnets before interacting with mainnet to avoid real costs and risks.
Pro tip
Add explicit error messages and retry logic around network calls to make debugging faster for both devs and users.

screens.title: From Web3.js Calls to Contract Interaction
screens.subtitle: How to create a contract instance and call methods safely

narration.text: Interacting with a smart contract through Web3. js requires two things: the contract's deployed address and its ABI — the interface that describes methods and events. You create a contract instance with new web3. eth. Contract(abi, address) and then call read-only methods with contract. methods. myMethod(...). call() and send state-changing transactions with contract. methods. myMethod(...). send({ from: account }). Remember that. call() is typically used for view functions and does not require gas, while. send() triggers a transaction that must be signed by a private key or an injected wallet. When sending, pass from and optionally gas and value fields. Always ensure the account you use has sufficient balance and that the provider you use supports signing; MetaMask injects a provider that will prompt the user to sign. For server-side signing, manage keys securely and avoid sending them to the browser. Also, verify ABI matches the deployed contract; mismatches are a frequent source of confusing failures. Test contract calls on Ganache before touching a testnet or mainnet. This staged approach reduces risk and clarifies the difference between reading state and changing it.

keyIdea.title: Contract interaction
keyIdea.text: Use ABI and address to create a contract instance, call view methods with .call(), and invoke transactions with .send() while ensuring account and provider support signing.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Contract Interaction
Create and use a contract
const contract = new web3.eth.Contract(abi, contractAddress);

// Read-only call
const value = await contract.methods.someView().call();

// State-changing transaction
await contract.methods.changeState(42).send({ from: accountAddress });
Use .call for view functions and .send for transactions that modify state. Ensure ABI and address are correct.
Signing
Injected wallets sign transactions in the browser. For backend signing, keep private keys on the server and never expose them to clients.
Gas & value
When sending a transaction, specify gas and value if required. Check account balance before sending to avoid failures.
Key Takeaway

Differentiate read-only .call() from state-changing .send(), and ensure your provider supports signing for transactions.

screens.title: Typical DApp Flow: Frontend to Smart Contract
screens.subtitle: A practical sequence from user action to on-chain effect

narration.text: A typical DApp flow begins with a user action in the frontend: clicking a button to transfer tokens or submit data. The frontend gathers input and asks the user to sign a transaction via an injected wallet or sends the data to a backend that will sign on its behalf. If using an injected wallet, the wallet prompts the user to confirm and signs the transaction locally. The signed transaction is then submitted to the connected Ethereum node through the provider. The node propagates the transaction to miners or validators and when included in a block, the blockchain state changes. The frontend can watch for confirmations via Web3. js subscriptions or by polling for the transaction receipt. For reads, the frontend calls contract methods directly without signing and receives immediate state. Designers must decide which operations require user signatures and which can happen as read-only UI updates. Testing this flow with Ganache and test accounts helps you catch UX and gas-related issues early. In practice, clearly communicating confirmation status and estimated wait times improves user trust during this asynchronous, multi-step process.

keyIdea.title: Flow insight
keyIdea.text: User action → optional signing (wallet) → node submission → block confirmation; use subscriptions or polling to confirm finality.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Typical DApp Flow
Frontend → Wallet → Node → Blockchain
A stepwise sequence from user action to on-chain change.
1
User triggers action in the UI.
2
Frontend requests signature via injected wallet or prepares payload for backend signing.
3
Signed transaction is submitted to a node through the provider.
4
Transaction is mined and state updates; frontend watches for confirmations.
UX note
Show clear status messages: pending, confirmed, failed. Users expect feedback for asynchronous transaction flows.
Testing tip
Use Ganache accounts for signing and repeated fast confirmations to iterate on the UX before deploying to testnet.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential concepts. First, a Decentralized Application separates frontend UI from on-chain smart contract logic. Put only the trust-critical rules on-chain and keep heavy or mutable data off-chain. Second, Web3. js is the JavaScript library that your frontend uses to call node RPCs, create contract instances, and submit transactions; it is the bridge between browser and blockchain. Third, an Ethereum node provides the RPC endpoints your Web3 instance needs to access blocks, accounts, and contract state; nodes can be local or hosted. Keep these three ideas in mind as the foundation for DApp design and development. Testing with a local node like Ganache and verifying getBlockNumber and getAccounts is a simple practical test that confirms your setup. These core concepts are the building blocks for learning contract interaction, signing flows, and provider selection in later lessons.

keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: DApps = frontend + smart contracts; Web3.js is the bridge; nodes provide the network access you need.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Key Concepts
Decentralized Application
Frontend paired with smart contracts for trust and immutability.
Web3.js
A JavaScript library that talks to nodes and enables contract calls and transactions.
Ethereum Node
A client that syncs blockchain state and exposes RPC endpoints for Web3.js to call.
Summary takeaway
Master these concepts to reliably connect your frontend to contracts, choose appropriate providers, and design DApps that balance trust, cost, and performance.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Providers & Async

narration.text: Two practical reminders to carry forward: provider choice and asynchronous discipline. First, select a provider that matches your needs: HTTP for straightforward reads and simple testing, WebSocket when you need live events and subscriptions, IPC for same-host server scenarios, and injected providers like MetaMask for secure user signing. Each provider has trade-offs in features and environment compatibility. Second, treat all Web3. js calls as asynchronous. Always await Promises or use. then/. catch, and design your UI to present loading and error states. These two habits — picking the right provider and handling async correctly — will prevent the majority of early development issues and make your DApp predictable and secure for users. Injected Providers

Async / Promises
